narrative:
The model estimates you have a 24% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a majority prediction, it is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of passing.

The three factors that most influenced this decision were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your history of one past class failure, and your reason for choosing this school. Wanting to continue studying after high school is the strongest factor. Every student who passed expressed a clear wish to pursue higher education; your answer of “no” pulled the prediction strongly toward failing. Your record of one previous failure was the second most important driver. Students who passed had zero past failures on average, so this history worked against you. Finally, choosing the school because it was close to home pushed the prediction in the opposite direction, slightly toward passing, because many successful students also chose it for practical reasons.

To improve, you should first reflect on your goals. If you can find motivation to aim for further education, your risk of failing would drop sharply. Reducing future absences, which are already more than four times the average of students who passed, and increasing your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend would also help. Taking the remedial courses seriously gives you a practical opportunity to address these gaps before the final exams.
